problem: Generic RAG (NaiveRAG, GraphRAG, LightRAG) lacks explicit spatial modeling, so on multi-goal VLN it suffers spatial hallucination and planning drift; traditional topological maps lack semantic memory and relational reasoning between goals.
motivation: Multi-goal VLN needs joint identification of several targets plus reasoning over their spatial constraints and visiting order. Vector-similarity retrieval ignores physical connectivity, and GraphRAG is too slow for navigation, so a queryable memory tying semantics to physical topology is needed.
key_idea: Build a dual-basis memory (low-level topological map plus high-level semantic forest) and use anchor-guided conditional retrieval with topological neighbor score boosting to localize multiple targets and plan their visiting order.
insight: The ablations show both memory bases matter: removing the semantic forest drops retrieval accuracy to 0.15 and removing the topological map drops it to 0.24, with success rates falling to 0.28 and 0.21 respectively (vs 0.65 full). The retrieval enhancements (spatial and neighbor) each cost roughly 0.07-0.11 in accuracy and about 0.34-0.37 in SR. Structured pruning keeps retrieval time (185-195 ms) close to LightRAG while GraphRAG needs 420-430 ms. Caveat: evaluation is on a small self-built AirSim dataset, so the evidence is limited.
method: Autonomous exploration: greedy frontier exploration on a 1.0 m grid with BFS clustering, collecting RGB, LiDAR and 6-DoF poses.
Instruction decomposition: an LLM parses the instruction into a subtask chain with spatial dependencies (A near B: anchor B, conditional A) and temporal dependencies (first A, then B).
Topological map: key pose nodes annotated with GPT-4o visual descriptions (spatial fingerprints); undirected edges added between nodes closer than 2.0 m.
Semantic forest: bottom-up agglomerative clustering on a fused spatial+semantic similarity, with an LLM summarizing child nodes into parent labels.

Two-stage anchor-guided retrieval: top-K global semantic recall, then neighborhood validation for the anchor with score 1/(1+d) and a Gaussian distance kernel; candidates without the anchor are pruned.
Topological neighbor boosting: S_boost = S_sem·(1+η·mean neighbor score) to propagate confidence from co-occurring neighbors.

Route planning: Dijkstra over the topological graph, then permutation search minimizing travel cost plus a semantic-order deviation penalty, with a closed-loop perception-planning-execution-reflection cycle.

setting.backbone: LLM for parsing/summarization (unspecified) + GPT-4o for node descriptions + text/visual embedding models (frozen)
setting.observation: RGB images, LiDAR point clouds, 6-DoF odometry poses, optional extra sensors (thermal/depth/NDVI)
setting.action_space: topological node waypoints executed by an assumed perfect local planner
setting.privileged: assumes a perfect local planner; the environment memory is pre-built offline via exploration before task execution

numbers.extra: custom dataset of 14 object-centric topological graphs (~80 nodes each); the split is not defined in the paper; values printed as fractions, e.g. SR 0.65
numbers.evidence: Table 2: RAGNav SR 0.65, 30.02 s, 16.13 m; Table 1 Text input retrieval accuracy 0.46

numbers_note: Only a self-built AirSim dataset is used; no standard VLN benchmark is reported. Accuracy and SR values are printed as fractions (0.65) though the column headers say %, so they are kept as printed. Retrieval accuracy for the Text+Location and Text+Location+Sensor inputs was 0.21 and 0.34.
results: On the custom AirSim benchmark RAGNav reaches an SR of 0.65 vs 0.52 for ReMEmbR and 0.42 for ETPNav, with the lowest time (30.02 s) and travel distance (16.13 m). Retrieval accuracy is 0.46 (Text) vs 0.17 for LightRAG, at 185 ms vs 420 ms for GraphRAG.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on a small self-built AirSim dataset with no standard VLN benchmarks, and few baselines.
Assumes a perfect local planner and a pre-built offline memory; no dynamic obstacle robustness or real-robot tests.
Retrieval accuracy is low in absolute terms (0.46, and drops to 0.21 when location is added), and the paper does not explain the drop.
